name: 24LC02BT-I_SN
title: 24AA02, 24LC02B, 24FC02: 2 Kbit (256 x 8) I2C serial EEPROM
summary: A family of 2 Kbit serial EEPROMs organised as 256 bytes and reached over a two-wire I2C-compatible bus, with an 8-byte page buffer, self-timed writes of 5 ms maximum and a write-protect pin that locks the whole array. 24AA02 works from 1.7 V, 24LC02B from 2.5 V (both 400 kHz) and 24FC02 from 1.7 V at 1 MHz; the address pins A0 to A2 have no internal connection. 24LC02BT-I/SN is the 24LC02B in an 8-lead SOIC, -40 °C to +85 °C, on tape and reel.
key_figures: 1 µA max (I-temp.); 3 µA (24FC02 E); 5 µA (24LC02B E)

The T in the order code is used for ordering only and is not marked on the part.

Marking codes: in 4A02T and 4L2BT the T is the temperature letter (I or E); NN is a two-character traceability code; YY is the last two digits of the year. 24AA02 and 24LC02B in SOT-23 carry a one-line marking, 24FC02 in SOT-23 a two-line marking.
PDIP and SOIC parts carry the part number itself, the temperature and package codes, the year and week and a traceability code (24LC02BI / SN e3 1922 / 13F on a SOIC).
Automotive-grade order codes are separate; Microchip supplies them on request.

operation.text: 2 Kbit of EEPROM arranged as 256 bytes in a single block, reached over a two-wire I2C-compatible bus. Writes are self-timed and take at most 5 ms for a single byte or a full 8-byte page. Rated for over one million erase/write cycles and over 200 years of retention. SCL and SDA have Schmitt-trigger inputs, and the output edge rate is controlled to limit ground bounce. Factory programming is offered.

24AA02 runs from 1.7 V to 5.5 V, industrial range only, with a 400 kHz clock above 2.5 V and 100 kHz below. 24LC02B runs from 2.5 V to 5.5 V at up to 400 kHz, industrial or extended range. 24FC02 runs from 1.7 V to 5.5 V at up to 1 MHz across the whole supply range, industrial or extended. Pins A0, A1 and A2 have no internal connection on any of them.
The memory is always a slave. A master drives SCL, decides who may use the bus and issues every Start and Stop. Either side can send or receive; the master sets the direction.

Idle: SDA and SCL both high. A transfer may begin only on an idle bus. Start: SDA falls while SCL is high; every command opens with one. Stop: SDA rises while SCL is high; every operation closes with one. Data: SDA must hold steady through each SCL high period and change only while SCL is low, one bit per clock; any SDA edge during SCL high is read as Start or Stop.

After each byte the receiver pulls SDA low through a ninth clock supplied by the master, keeping it low for the whole high time of that clock and meeting the setup and hold times. When reading, the master marks the final byte by leaving that ninth bit high (no acknowledge); the memory then releases SDA so the master can send Stop. While an internal write cycle is running the memory acknowledges nothing.

The first byte after Start is the control byte: the 4-bit code 1010, then three block-select bits that the 24XX02 ignores (don't care), then the R/W bit (1 = read, 0 = write). The code and the three bits together form the slave address. When the memory sees a matching control byte it acknowledges and takes the read or write path. For a write, the next byte is the word address; all eight bits are used, covering 00h to FFh.

Master sends Start, the control byte with R/W = 0, the word address and one data byte, the memory acknowledging each; the master then sends Stop. Stop launches the internal write cycle, and the memory does not acknowledge until it ends.

Starts like a byte write, but the master keeps sending data bytes, up to eight, before Stop. They collect in an on-chip page buffer and are programmed together after Stop. After each byte the low three bits of the address pointer step up by one while the upper five stay fixed, so a page is eight bytes on an 8-byte boundary. More than eight bytes, or a run that would run past an 8-byte boundary, wraps to the start of the same page and overwrites what was loaded earlier there; firmware has to keep a page write inside one page. Only the last eight bytes sent are kept.
WP at VCC protects the whole array (00h-FFh) against writes; reads still work. WP at VSS allows writes. The pin must be driven or tied, never left open.

Since the memory ignores the bus while it programs, the master can detect the end of a write cycle and use the bus sooner: right after the Stop that starts the write, send Start and a write control byte (R/W = 0). No acknowledge means the cycle is still running, so repeat; an acknowledge means it has finished and the next read or write can follow at once.

An internal address pointer holds the address after the last byte accessed by a read or a write. A control byte with R/W = 1 makes the memory acknowledge and send the byte at that address (n + 1 after an access at n). The master answers with no acknowledge and a Stop.

To read a chosen address, the master first loads the pointer with a dummy write: Start, control byte with R/W = 0, word address. Then, instead of Stop, it sends a repeated Start and the control byte with R/W = 1. The memory acknowledges and sends the byte; the master returns no acknowledge and a Stop.

Begins as a current address or random read, but the master acknowledges each byte it receives, and the memory sends the byte at the next address each time. The pointer advances by one per byte, so the whole array can be read out in a single transfer. The master ends it with no acknowledge and Stop.
SCL and SDA each have a Schmitt trigger and a spike filter (TSP up to 50 ns) so short glitches on a noisy bus are ignored.
SDA is open drain and needs a pull-up resistor to VCC: about 10 kΩ for a 100 kHz bus, about 2 kΩ for 400 kHz or 1 MHz.
On TDFN and UDFN parts the exposed pad may be tied to VSS or left unconnected.
Reading draws at most 1 mA and writing at most 3 mA at 5.5 V and 400 kHz. Standby is at most 1 µA on industrial parts, 3 µA on extended-range 24FC02 and 5 µA on extended-range 24LC02B.
AEC-Q100 qualified for automotive use; ESD protection over 4000 V on all pins; RoHS compliant.
